first_use_terms.first_context: The cardiovascular system moves blood between the heart, the lungs and the body's tissues. Perfusion is the passage of blood through a tissue's vascular bed. Ischemia means that the blood supply is inadequate for the tissue's requirements. The relevant requirement is functional: a visible opening does not establish an adequate supply of oxygen and nutrients.

first_use_terms.first_context: The course introduces its subject through historical cardiovascular disease statistics. Those statistics must retain their dates and denominators. A fraction of all deaths attributed to one cause is not the probability that a person with that disease will die. A case fatality fraction divides deaths among cases by the number of cases; an incidence rate divides new events by accumulated time at risk. These quantities can change in different directions.

first_use_terms.first_context: Wall shear stress describes the tangential loading associated with blood flow at the wall. Circumferential normal stress , often called hoop stress, describes tensile or compressive loading along the wall's circumferential direction. It is a stress inside the solid wall. Pressure can produce hoop tension without producing the same quantity as fluid wall shear. Keeping those two stresses separate is essential when interpreting the review lecture's examples.

first_use_terms.first_context: Mechanotransduction is the conversion of a mechanical stimulus into a cellular response. It supplies a biological reason to compute stresses, but a computed field is not itself a measured cellular outcome. Dai and colleagues' 2004 experiment applied arterial shear-stress waveforms to cultured human endothelial cells and observed differences in cellular organization and gene expression. The experiment links a controlled mechanical input to biological responses under its culture conditions. It does not make one scalar shear value a complete predictor of plaque formation in a person.

first_use_terms.first_context: An aneurysm, a localized enlargement of a vessel, exposes another boundary. Changing the assumed blood viscosity can change a simulated wall-shear map. Predicting wall rupture additionally requires a model of the solid wall's loading, geometry, material strength and disease-related changes. The fluid's tangential traction and the wall's tensile failure criterion are different objects. Agreement between two flow simulations is not a validation of a rupture prediction.

first_use_terms.first_context: The continuum approximation makes local balances possible. It does not choose the material law. A Newtonian description makes viscous stress proportional to the instantaneous deformation rate. A shear-dependent description allows apparent viscosity to change with that rate. A multiphase description tracks constituent phases separately. Each adds assumptions beyond a smooth velocity field. The next chapter develops the kinematic objects needed to make those choices precise.

first_use_terms.first_context: The lecture introduces a Knudsen-number analogy: a molecular mean free path divided by a macroscopic length. That ratio is useful in assessing rarefied-gas continuum approximations. A red blood cell is a deformable constituent of a dense suspension, so a gas-like molecular mean free path and a universal numerical cutoff do not by themselves establish the validity of a whole-blood model. Cell size, spatial averaging, migration, confinement and the constitutive law must also be considered. The model used for a large vessel can therefore be inappropriate for resolving a single cell passing through a narrow capillary.

first_use_terms.first_context: Consider one tissue bed supplied through a narrowed vessel. Its cells continue to consume oxygen. We want to determine which observations constrain delivery, which assumptions turn anatomy into a calculation, and where that calculation stops. The recurring example is deliberately simple: a long circular tube supplying a well-mixed tissue compartment. Its purpose is to expose the assumptions that a detailed simulation can otherwise conceal.

first_use_terms.first_context: Anatomy describes structures and their relationships. Physiology describes how those structures function. Structure–function complementarity means that geometry, composition and organization help enable a function. It is an explanatory relationship to investigate, rather than a proof that every observed feature is optimal for every possible objective.

first_use_terms.first_context: Four intervention examples reveal different mechanical tasks. Balloon angioplasty changes the geometry of a narrowed artery while loading its wall. A bypass graft introduces an alternative path for blood. A ventricular assist device supports a ventricle, one of the heart’s pumping chambers. It supplies pumping work while exposing blood to a new flow environment. Mechanical thrombectomy engages and removes a clot in selected cases of acute ischemic stroke; the FDA device definition makes that scope explicit. These examples motivate models of contact, deformation, fluid flow and transport. They do not imply that the same model decides when each intervention is appropriate.

first_use_terms.first_context: An artery carries blood away from the heart; a vein carries it toward the heart. The definition concerns direction relative to the heart, not oxygen content. Pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs, and pulmonary veins return it toward the left atrium. The systemic path then carries blood from the left ventricle through tissues and back to the right side of the heart.

first_use_terms.first_context: Blood contains liquid plasma and formed elements, including red cells, white cells and platelets. Mature human red cells cannot divide and lack mitochondria, but they remain metabolically active. They obtain usable chemical energy through glycolysis, the breakdown of glucose. Direct metabolomic and proteomic measurements of red-cell energy pathways make that distinction explicit. Describing a cell as an oxygen carrier does not mean it is an inert particle that consumes no nutrients.

first_use_terms.first_context: A small mathematical example makes the limitation precise. A dot over a quantity denotes its derivative with respect to time. Let \(e(t)\) be a dimensionless deviation from a reference condition, \(d(t)\) an externally imposed disturbance rate in \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), and \(k>0\) a constant in \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). The original teaching model \(\dot e=d-ke\) gives \(e(t)=e(0)e^{-kt}\) when \(d=0\), so deviations decay. With constant nonzero \(d\), the equilibrium is \(e=d/k\), which is generally not zero. Negative feedback can reduce a deviation without eliminating it; delays, saturation and additional state variables can change the conclusion. This scalar model does not represent the full physiology of insulin or coagulation.

first_use_terms.first_context: The two circuits are connected in series. In a steady model with no shunt and no accumulation of blood in either circuit, conservation requires the same mean flow through both. Different pressures are compatible with the same flow because the two circuits have different resistances and pumping loads. The inference that the left ventricle pumps farther is incomplete: pressure, geometry, material properties and loading all enter a mechanical explanation.

first_use_terms.first_context: For the mechanical part, idealize the supply segment as a straight, rigid circular tube of radius \(a\gt0\) and length \(L\gt0\), both measured in metres. Assume steady flow, meaning no time dependence, and laminar motion, excluding turbulent fluctuations in this model. A fully developed axial velocity profile does not change along the straight tube. Let the fluid be incompressible and Newtonian, with constant dynamic viscosity \(\mu\gt0\) in \(\mathrm{Pa\,s}\). Neglect gravity and other body forces. These assumptions remove pulsation, wall deformation, cellular migration, entrance losses and the three-dimensional geometry of a short stenosis.

first_use_terms.first_context: An atrium is a receiving chamber; a ventricle is a discharge chamber with a substantial muscular wall. The right atrium receives systemic venous return, the right ventricle ejects toward the lungs, the left atrium receives pulmonary venous return, and the left ventricle ejects into the aorta. The septa separate the right and left sides in the ordinary anatomy considered here. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins toward it; pulmonary vessels show why those names do not mean oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor.

first_use_terms.first_context: Two ventricles can show the same decrease in chamber volume while sending different amounts of blood forward. A pressure trace can remain high in an artery while the ventricle that filled it has already relaxed. To understand either observation, we need the chambers, valves and vessels as a connected mechanical system.

first_use_terms.first_context: Three wall terms deserve distinct definitions. The endocardium lines the chambers; its surface includes endothelium continuous with vascular endothelium. The myocardium is the contracting cardiac-muscle layer. The epicardium is the outer heart surface, associated with the visceral layer of serous pericardium. The enclosing pericardial sac and its lubricated interface reduce friction during motion. A thin fluid-filled interface can reduce tangential friction while still transmitting normal pressure; lubrication does not imply that the heart has no external mechanical constraints.

first_use_terms.first_context: The cardiovascular system transports blood so that exchange at tissue microvessels can supply nutrients and remove metabolic products. The heart generates mechanical pressure work; the vessels distribute and store blood; the blood transports matter and energy. The heart's own myocardium also requires a coronary blood supply. Pumping blood through a cavity is not the same process as delivering oxygen to all the cells in its wall.

first_use_terms.first_context: The right atrioventricular valve is the tricuspid valve; the left is the mitral, typically two-leaflet valve. Chordae tendineae connect their leaflets to papillary muscles and help prevent leaflet prolapse when ventricular pressure rises. They do not operate as ropes that actively pull the valve open. The pulmonary and aortic valves are semilunar outlet valves, typically with three cusps, and have a different supporting arrangement. NHLBI's blood-flow account identifies the four chamber-to-vessel connections and their directional roles.

first_use_terms.first_context: Our running example is a left ventricle connected to an atrial reservoir through a mitral valve and to an arterial reservoir through an aortic valve. We begin with ideal one-way valves, then ask what changes when a valve leaks or the downstream load increases. The purpose is to connect anatomy to conservation, pressure differences and work, rather than infer function from one isolated number.

first_use_terms.first_context: Systole denotes the contraction phase and diastole the relaxation/filling phase, with the chamber specified. Atrial systole occurs during late ventricular diastole. Ventricular systole includes isovolumic contraction as well as ejection. Electrical activation coordinates the sequence; a prescribed mechanical activation schedule is an assumption, not an explanation of how the conduction system generates it. The NHLBI account of the heartbeat describes that coordinating electrical role.

first_use_terms.first_context: End-diastolic volume, EDV, is the chamber volume at the end of filling; end-systolic volume, ESV, is the volume remaining at the end of ejection. EDV is a state reached in the particular beat, not a fixed maximum anatomical capacity. The heart does not begin to contract merely because an incompressible container has become completely full. Active electrical–mechanical coordination changes wall force generation, and the pressure inequalities then govern valve behavior.

first_use_terms.first_context: Stenosis and regurgitation change different parts of this model. Stenosis restricts the available forward opening and can increase the pressure loss needed for a given flow. Regurgitation permits appreciable reverse flow when the valve should exclude it. Ranking every left-sided lesion as more serious than every right-sided lesion does not follow from anatomy alone: both circuits participate in a coupled circulation. This model provides no individual indication for valve replacement.

first_use_terms.first_context: Zero pressure–volume boundary work during an ideal isovolumic phase does not mean zero biochemical energy use. Active tissue can generate force, redistribute internal strain, dissipate energy and consume adenosine triphosphate (ATP) , a molecule supplying chemical energy to cellular processes, while total cavity volume is fixed. Pressure–volume area, local material stress–strain work and whole-organ metabolic expenditure are distinct objects. Converting one into another requires an additional model and measurements.

first_use_terms.first_context: Isotropy means that rotating material directions relative to a prescribed deformation does not change the constitutive response. Transverse isotropy retains one preferred material axis but requires rotational symmetry throughout the plane perpendicular to it. Merely finding the same modulus along two selected directions is insufficient to establish all those symmetries. Orthotropy has three mutually orthogonal material symmetry directions/planes and permits distinct responses associated with them. It is more specific than the statement that properties differ in three arbitrary directions.

first_use_terms.first_context: At a material point, define orthonormal reference directions $\mathbf f_0,\mathbf s_0,\mathbf n_0$ for fibre, sheet and sheet-normal organization. A spatially varying fibre field might be $\mathbf f_0(X_3)=\cos\theta(X_3)\mathbf e_1+\sin\theta(X_3)\mathbf e_2$. Its changing angle describes structural variation through the wall. Heterogeneity concerns variation with position; anisotropy concerns dependence on direction at one position. A homogeneous anisotropic slab and a heterogeneous isotropic slab are both possible mathematical materials.

first_use_terms.first_context: For our running slab take $\mathbf f_0=\mathbf e_1$ and $\mathbf s_0=\mathbf e_2$, using orthonormal Cartesian basis vectors. Let $\mathbf F=\partial\mathbf x/\partial\mathbf X$ be the dimensionless deformation gradient from reference position $\mathbf X$ to current position $\mathbf x$, and set $\mathbf C=\mathbf F^T\mathbf F$. Relevant dimensionless invariants are $I_1=\operatorname{tr}\mathbf C$, $I_{4f}=\mathbf f_0\cdot\mathbf C\mathbf f_0$, $I_{4s}=\mathbf s_0\cdot\mathbf C\mathbf s_0$, and $I_{8fs}=\mathbf f_0\cdot\mathbf C\mathbf s_0$. Fibre stretch is $\lambda_f=\sqrt{I_{4f}}$. The last invariant measures the dot product of deformed reference unit fibre and sheet vectors; it is zero when those deformed vectors remain perpendicular.

first_use_terms.first_context: Near-incompressibility means the material's volume changes little under the conditions modeled. In a small-strain isotropic comparison, a bulk modulus $K$ much larger than shear modulus $\mu$ makes volumetric strain small relative to typical distortional strains. Under uniform compressive pressure $p$, the linearized estimate is $\Delta V/V\simeq-p/K$. With illustrative $K=10\,\mathrm{MPa}$ and $p=10\,\mathrm{kPa}$, its magnitude is0.001. This does not establish a universal ratio for every perfused myocardial specimen.

first_use_terms.first_context: For this incompressible hyperelastic solid, the full nominal stress includes the constraint multiplier: $\mathbf P=\partial W/\partial\mathbf F-pJ\mathbf F^{-T}$. Along an admissible increment, $dJ=J\mathbf F^{-T}:d\mathbf F=0$, so the multiplier contributes $-p\,dJ=0$ to the work and $\mathbf P:d\mathbf F=dW$. A quasistatic path passes through successive equilibrium states with inertia neglected. Around a closed such path returning every state variable to its initial value, $\oint\mathbf P:d\mathbf F=\oint dW=0$. An observed loading/unloading loop with nonzero area therefore requires dissipation, an evolving internal state, separate protocol-specific pseudoelastic branches, or another mechanism beyond that single reversible energy. Calling the curve nonlinear does not by itself account for hysteresis.

first_use_terms.first_context: Blood contains red cells, white cells and platelets suspended in plasma. Red cells and white cells are cells; platelets are fragments released by megakaryocytes , large platelet-producing cells found in bone marrow. The collective expression formed elements does not mean that every member is a noncellular object. Mature mammalian red cells lack nuclei and mitochondria, but retain membrane transport, enzymes and a metabolism. The lecture's structural economy argument should therefore be read as specialization for transport, not as biological inertness.

first_use_terms.first_context: Hemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly. A hemoglobin tetramer can bind four oxygen molecules, one per heme; after one site binds, three sites remain, not another four. Cooperative affinity is not equivalent to irreversible loading. Oxygen partial pressure, acidity, temperature and other chemical conditions influence the binding state. Let $G=-dp/dz>0$, radius $R$, no slip, negligible body force and the scalar Casson relation above. Axial momentum fixes $|\tau_{rz}|=Gr/2$ independently of the viscosity law. Its unidirectional equation is $\rho\partial_tu=G(t)+\mu r^{-1}\partial_r(r\partial_ru)$, with zero wall velocity. The parabolic maximum principle prevents a first negative interior minimum: diffusion and forcing there cannot drive the value down through zero. Thus inertia alone is not an explanation for reversal under these particular assumptions. The scope of the comparison matters as much as the signal.

first_use_terms.first_context: For a simple drag closure, take $\mathbf f_c=-\beta(\mathbf v_c-\mathbf v_p)$ and $\mathbf f_p=-\mathbf f_c$, $\beta\ge0$. The forces cancel in total linear momentum, but their combined mechanical power is $-\beta|\mathbf v_c-\mathbf v_p|^2\le0$. Thus internal interaction can dissipate energy while conserving momentum. Here $\beta$ has units Pa s/m$^2$. With $\beta=10^6$ and speed difference $0.01\;\mathrm{m/s}$, the loss is $100\;\mathrm{W/m^3}$.

first_use_terms.first_context: The code implements a conservative finite-volume check on a dimensionless channel. Put $q_i=c_i e^{\chi\phi_i}$ and face flux $j_{i+1/2}=-D_c e^{-\chi\phi_{i+1/2}}(q_{i+1}-q_i)/\Delta y$. Adjacent cells share the same face flux with opposite signs, so total amount telescopes exactly under zero boundary flux. The explicit step is chosen small enough that every update is a nonnegative weighted combination of neighboring concentrations. It preserves positivity and approaches the stated discrete equilibrium. Mass conservation, positivity and equilibrium are separate checks; any one alone would be insufficient.

first_use_terms.first_context: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it. These names concern direction of transport, not an absolute oxygen label: pulmonary vessels provide the familiar reversal of the usual systemic oxygen association. Arterioles connect the distributing arteries to exchange networks, and capillaries drain through venules into veins. The NCI vessel-structure resource describes this hierarchy and its differences in wall construction.

first_use_terms.first_context: A longer residence time can help exchange, but slow flow does not by itself prove complete equilibration. For transverse diffusion distance $\delta$ and diffusivity $D_m$, compare $\delta^2/D_m$ with transit time $L/\bar u$. Their ratio $D_mL/(\bar u\delta^2)$ measures the available diffusion time on this simplified basis. Permeability, surface area, chemical binding and tissue demand also matter. The source's exchange-site picture is a functional motivation, not a complete oxygen transport model.

first_use_terms.first_context: Pressure at a location is a scalar field $p(\mathbf x,t)$; a pressure gradient is force per volume, $-\nabla p$. A time trace ranging between two pressures does not supply a spatial gradient without a distance and a second location. Likewise, the number $80$ in an illustrative 120/80 pressure pair is not automatically the axial pressure drop driving flow along a given segment. A uniform offset in both ends' pressure changes wall loading without changing their difference.

first_use_terms.first_context: The wall responds strongly to transmural pressure $\Delta p=p_i-p_o$, with internal and external pressures specified at the same axial level and time. The flow responds to spatial differences of pressure and other body/inertial forces. Consider a vessel with $p_i=15$ kPa and $p_o=2$ kPa. Its transmural load is 13 kPa. Raising both by 5 kPa leaves this difference unchanged. A flow model that uses only an upstream absolute pressure still needs downstream and surrounding conditions.

first_use_terms.first_context: The lecture illustrates attenuation of pulsations through the network. This is a useful trend, not a guarantee of exactly steady flow in every arteriole, capillary or vein. Compliance, distributed resistance, inertance and wave reflections all affect the waveform. Respiratory variation, vessel motion and local regulation add further timescales. It is safer to say that a mean-flow approximation may be adequate for a specified observable than to declare an entire vessel class mathematically steady.

first_use_terms.first_context: In a representative artery, the intima is the inner layer containing the blood-facing endothelial cell lining. The media is the middle layer containing smooth muscle and elastic structure. The adventitia is the outer connective layer attaching the vessel to surrounding tissue. Elastin, collagen, smooth muscle and other constituents differ among layers and along the network. Those differences motivate region-specific constitutive parameters and sometimes different model forms. They also make a single scalar modulus an incomplete description of large-deformation behavior.

first_use_terms.first_context: This cancellation does not make posture irrelevant. Transmural pressure compares local luminal pressure with the surrounding tissue pressure. Compliant vessels can change area and stored volume; venous segments may approach collapse, and the reference level of a pressure measurement matters. A constant-density closed-loop gravitational integral $\oint\rho g\,dz=0$ removes a net gravitational head around the full loop, but does not remove local gravitational loading or its effect on storage. A lumped model with no height coordinate must represent such redistribution through an explicit additional state or a declared disturbance. It cannot acquire a posture mechanism simply by calling one coefficient “gravity.”
